title: Conflict of Interest

jokes.text: is he making this up as he goes along? / He's telling an American story. / I thought he was gonna do his hit. / I think he's doing his bong hit.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Beck is improvising. Another person defends the performance as 'telling an American story.' A third person says they expected Beck to do his hit.
jokes.punchline: 'I think he's doing his bong hit.' — wordplay on 'hit' (song vs. marijuana hit) delivered deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A tight, economy-driven wordplay joke that works on two levels simultaneously — the confusion about Beck's rambling set and the drug implication. The delivery is very on-brand for the show's dry wit. Not exceptional but well-constructed.

dialogue.line: is he making this up as he goes along?
He's telling an American story.
I thought he was gonna do his hit.
I think he's doing his bong hit.

jokes.text: odd booking for the show, wouldn't you say? / Well, Paula, you know, she was looking for something different. She wanted something hip. / Yeah. What about Harry Connick, Jr.? I thought he was supposed to be on. / Oh, Harry Connick, Jr., dear sir, is not handled by Stevie Grant.
jokes.setup: Artie notes that Beck is an odd booking. Larry defends Paula's choice as 'hip.' Larry then pivots to asking about the more mainstream Harry Connick Jr.
jokes.punchline: Artie's clipped, arch explanation that Harry Connick Jr. is 'not handled by Stevie Grant' — implying the booking is purely personal/transactional rather than artistic.
jokes.explanation: This is textbook Larry Sanders Show comedy — the punchline is institutional rot delivered as casual information. Artie's formal diction ('dear sir') makes the cynicism even funnier. High character integration because only Artie would deliver this observation with that particular bored authority.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So my agent's fucking my booker?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, good to know.

jokes.text: So my agent's fucking my booker? Yes.
jokes.setup: Artie explains that Stevie and Paula are 'an item,' implying that bookings are being influenced by a romantic relationship.
jokes.punchline: Larry distills the entire situation into 'So my agent's fucking my booker?' — reframing the professional/romantic conflict into a single blunt, transactional sentence, answered with a flat 'Yes.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best line and one of the show's signature moves: Larry's paranoid, self-centered worldview condenses a complicated situation into a single sentence that's simultaneously accurate and reductive. The word 'fucking' does triple duty — literal, professional betrayal, and vulgarity as comedy weapon. The flat 'Yes' confirmation makes it land even harder. Near-perfect economy. Justifies the 8+ score easily.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: but not a hillbilly from outer space

jokes.text: I'd love to watch him from the mosh pit, and we are in search of fresh faces with a point of view, but not a hillbilly from outer space.
jokes.setup: Paula defends Beck as fresh and exciting talent with a lollapalooza following.
jokes.punchline: 'but not a hillbilly from outer space' — Paula's own description undercuts her defense of Beck, revealing her ambivalence about a booking she championed.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny image — 'hillbilly from outer space' is a perfect two-word visual for Beck's mid-90s aesthetic, and it's funnier that it comes from the person who booked him. The self-contradicting defense is a sharp characterization beat.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Granted, he's no John tesh

jokes.text: Granted, he's no John Tesh, but he's got the lollapalooza following and Letterman's people have been all over him.
jokes.setup: Paula is defending Beck's cultural relevance to skeptical producers.
jokes.punchline: 'he's no John Tesh' — invoking the lamest possible comparison to tepidly praise Beck, which itself is both a dig at John Tesh and an oddly deflating compliment.
jokes.explanation: The John Tesh reference is a very specific mid-90s industry joke — the blandest of mainstream acts used as a baseline. Functional insider comedy that rewards the industry-savvy viewer. The Letterman name-drop adds competitive anxiety that's central to the show's DNA.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I love Sally, but I've seen miss struthers up here one more time this month.

jokes.text: Who is Beck's agent? / Stevie Grant. / And Jake Johannsen? Stevie. / Ed Begley Jr.? [pause] / Those names have nothing to do with my relationship.
jokes.setup: Larry starts asking whose agent represents which guests, systematically building a case.
jokes.punchline: Paula's defensive deflection only after the third name makes the pattern undeniable — the pause before 'Those names have nothing to do with my relationship' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders escalation structure: the rule of three used to build a damning pattern before the deflection. The rhythm is tight — each name answered in one word ('Stevie') until the dam breaks. Paula's denial is perfectly timed and only makes her look more guilty. The joke is structural as much as verbal.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Well, you know, my hooker days are over.

jokes.text: He also has several shit clients as well. / I love Sally, but I've seen Miss Struthers up here one more time this month.
jokes.setup: Artie concedes that Stevie has good clients but pivots immediately.
jokes.punchline: Artie's fond-but-exasperated 'I love Sally, but I've seen Miss Struthers up here one more time this month' — the 'one more time' construction implies Struthers has been overbooked while simultaneously not quite finishing the threat.
jokes.explanation: Very Artie — the 'I love Sally' setup makes the complaint feel almost reluctant, which is funnier than a straight dismissal. Sally Struthers as the emblem of a 'shit client' is a pointed but affectionate industry dig. The incomplete threat ('one more time this month') is a nice comic fragment.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Ha ha! You are the king! King Kong! Ha ha ha ha!

jokes.text: He said 'shit' in the middle of one of the songs. Are you aware of that? / He's an artist. / Well, I'm sure 'shit' rhymes with a lot of things.
jokes.setup: Larry complains to Stevie that Beck said 'shit' during the performance. Stevie defends him as an artist.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response — 'Well, I'm sure shit rhymes with a lot of things' — is a non-sequitur defense that concedes the artistic point while still being baffled, perfectly capturing Larry's mix of prudishness and self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The line is quintessential Larry — he's not quite defending Beck, not quite condemning him, just muttering something that reveals his total confusion about whether art excuses vulgarity on his show. The rhyme observation is a non-sequitur that's funnier for making no real point. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Which ones? The ones who can act.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, look, I've got a lot of musical acts, by the way. You know, say the word and I can get you hole. / Well, you know, my hooker days are over.
jokes.setup: Stevie offers to book the band Hole. Larry mishears or deliberately plays on the double meaning of 'hole.'
jokes.punchline: 'Well, you know, my hooker days are over.' — Larry interprets 'hole' as sexual slang and makes a self-deprecating reference to a past he implies he has, then both men crack up.
jokes.explanation: The wordplay on Hole (Courtney Love's band) is a bit predictable but Larry's response — 'my hooker days are over' — is a funny non-sequitur that implies a history and also gets the two men bonding over the joke. The chemistry between Garry Shandling and the actor playing Stevie sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: The little guy, the hyper guy? Mm-hmm. I don't think so. He's more of a conan o'brien act. Conan won't put him on.

jokes.text: Ha ha! You are the king! King Kong! Ha ha ha ha!
jokes.setup: Stevie reacts to Larry's 'hooker days' joke with explosive, sycophantic laughter.
jokes.punchline: The absurdly over-the-top 'King Kong!' — Stevie's agent-brain can't stop at 'King,' he escalates to 'King Kong' for no clear reason, revealing that his flattery is performative and slightly unhinged.
jokes.explanation: This is character comedy gold for the agent archetype — the laugh that's too big, the compliment that goes one step too far. 'King Kong' as a term of praise is so specific and odd that it becomes a running thread in the episode. The rewatch bonus is because this phrase pays off later.

dialogue.speaker: Peng Lee
dialogue.line: About American soldier push big elephant out of plane. Very funny.

jokes.text: Jennifer Aniston would be amazing. Can you get her? / Yeah, absolutely. I represent half the cast of Friends. / Which ones? The ones who can act.
jokes.setup: Paula asks if Stevie can get Jennifer Aniston. He brags about representing half the Friends cast.
jokes.punchline: 'The ones who can act.' — Stevie's smug qualifier implies he's ranking his own clients against each other, which is both a dig at half the Friends cast and a reveal of his total lack of filter.
jokes.explanation: A snappy two-beat exchange with a clean setup/punchline structure. The punchline is notably economical — four words that do a lot of work, implying both an industry ranking and personal arrogance. The Friends cast-ranking angle is a sharp insider joke for 1995.

dialogue.speaker: Peng Lee
dialogue.line: I give it 3 fortune... 4 fortune cookie. Highest rating.

jokes.text: Hey, do you have a spot for Andy Kindler? / Who's Andy Kindler? He's a comic. The little guy, the hyper guy? / Mm-hmm. I don't think so. He's more of a Conan O'Brien act. / Conan won't put him on.
jokes.setup: Stevie tries to get Andy Kindler on the show as a quid pro quo for Jennifer Aniston.
jokes.punchline: 'He's more of a Conan O'Brien act. / Conan won't put him on.' — Paula's dismissal and Stevie's reveal that even Conan won't book him is a comedy of diminishing returns, with Kindler being described as too small for everyone.
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is elegant: Paula categorizes Kindler as a 'Conan act' (a step down from Larry's show), and Stevie's one-line reveal that Conan also won't have him is a perfect deflating follow-up. The specificity of Andy Kindler — a real comedian who really did struggle for TV exposure — adds insider texture.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: What is it with the Chinese guy? He's on once a week and he's not funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Why don't you tell Larry?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna tell him.

jokes.text: Oh, yes. Tonight I'm going to review Operation Dumbo Drop. / Right. That is the movie where the elephant is... / Yes. About American soldier push big elephant out of plane. Very funny.
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the recurring movie critic segment with Peng Lee, a Chinese restaurant owner with broken English.
jokes.punchline: Peng Lee's description of Operation Dumbo Drop — 'American soldier push big elephant out of plane. Very funny.' — is a bizarre précis that is itself funnier than the movie and delivered with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is layered — Peng Lee's broken English synopsis of a bad movie, delivered earnestly. It's mildly funny but sits in uncomfortable territory (the show itself will later address whether this bit is exploitative). The craft is limited by the fact that the humor relies heavily on the accent rather than wit.

dialogue.speaker: Peng Lee
dialogue.line: Very bad for hemorrhoid.

jokes.text: Is it funny? / Absolutely. Very, very funny. / I give it 3 fortune... 4 fortune cookie. Highest rating.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Operation Dumbo Drop is actually a comedy.
jokes.punchline: Peng Lee's rating system: fortune cookies, and his upgrade mid-sentence from 3 to 4 — 'highest rating' — delivered with utter sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The fortune cookie rating system is a clever absurdist touch, and the self-correction mid-rating (3 to 4) adds a spontaneous quality that makes Peng Lee feel like a real person rather than a pure caricature. Still sits in uncomfortable stereotype territory.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I can't do this with Larry watching me. It gives me the creeps.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Doing it in front of my clients turns me on. I feel my power.

jokes.text: What is it with the Chinese guy? He's on once a week and he's not funny. / I know. / Why don't you tell Larry? / I'm not gonna tell him.
jokes.setup: Backstage, two people watch the Peng Lee segment on a monitor.
jokes.punchline: Artie's blunt 'He's not funny' followed by the immediate deflection of responsibility — 'Why don't you tell Larry? / I'm not gonna tell him.' Everyone agrees but no one will confront Larry.
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly meta joke: the show is commenting on its own bit through the characters. Everyone backstage has the same reaction the audience has, and the comedy of no one wanting to tell Larry is both a character joke and an institutional critique. Very Larry Sanders — the show's self-awareness about bad segments is itself a comedy device.

dialogue.speaker: Peng Lee
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I, uh, suspect lately our pork chop dishes, they suffer. Nobody order pork chop dishes.

jokes.text: Also the seat was broken. The seat was broken. Very bad for hemorrhoid.
jokes.setup: Peng Lee continues his movie review of Operation Dumbo Drop.
jokes.punchline: Completely out of nowhere, he pivots to the broken seat at the movie theater and its impact on his hemorrhoid — a totally unexpected personal detail that has nothing to do with the movie.
jokes.explanation: The best of the Peng Lee material. The hemorrhoid reveal is completely unexpected within a movie review and the doubling down ('the seat was broken. Very bad for hemorrhoid.') gives it perfect rhythm. Larry's pivot to make it a 'movie tip' is a good straight-man recovery.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, man, this is hilarious, don't you think? Artie? Don't you think this is hilarious? It's terrific. I'm enjoying it.

jokes.text: Are you talking about your own or just in general? Is that a movie tip from... we've gotten a little movie tip from the far east.
jokes.setup: Peng Lee announces the broken seat was 'very bad for hemorrhoid.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's confused pivot — first asking for clarification ('your own or just in general?'), then desperately reframing it as a 'movie tip from the far east' — is Larry doing live show triage.
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy: the host trying desperately to save face on live television while being derailed by an uncontrollable segment. 'A little movie tip from the far east' is both condescending and desperately optimistic — very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tell her to clean around me.

jokes.text: What? / I can't do this with Larry watching me. It gives me the creeps. / Doing it in front of my clients turns me on. I feel my power. / Just turn it off.
jokes.setup: Paula and Stevie are apparently watching the show from somewhere backstage. Paula is uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: 'Doing it in front of my clients turns me on. I feel my power.' — Stevie's revelation that watching his clients perform gives him a power-trip sexual thrill is a deeply strange and funny insight into the agent psyche.
jokes.explanation: This line cuts to the heart of the show's Hollywood satire — agents as power-hungry voyeurs who monetize other people's talent. 'I feel my power' is both funny and genuinely unsettling, which is the Larry Sanders sweet spot. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yes, sweetie, I do. I'm an addict.

jokes.text: A movie called Babe. That's the movie about the talking pig, isn't it? / Yes. / Is it funny? Did you enjoy it? / Yeah, but I suspect lately our pork chop dishes, they suffer. Nobody order pork chop dishes.
jokes.setup: Peng Lee reviews Babe, the talking pig movie.
jokes.punchline: Peng Lee connects the film's impact on his actual restaurant business — audiences who saw the sympathetic pig stopped ordering pork chops. A real-world economic consequence of a movie.
jokes.explanation: This is the best Peng Lee joke and one of the episode's strongest. The premise is genuinely original — a Chinese restaurant owner who moonlights as a movie critic gets hurt by the movies he reviews. The cause-and-effect logic (sympathetic pig → declining pork sales) is absurd but completely coherent. 'Nobody order pork chop dishes' is a perfect, specific punchline. Justifies 8+ because the comedic concept is truly novel and the character integration is complete — only this specific character setup could produce this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Fuck him, he doesn't know. He's the one who swore ovitz wasn't leaving.

jokes.text: Oh, man, this is hilarious, don't you think? / Artie? / Don't you think this is hilarious? / It's terrific. I'm enjoying it. / We should do this more often. I mean it. / Absolutely.
jokes.setup: Larry turns to Artie expecting enthusiastic agreement that the Peng Lee segment is killing.
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'It's terrific. I'm enjoying it.' — delivered with no energy, following his earlier backstage verdict of 'He's not funny.' The gap between what Larry wants to hear and what Artie actually thinks is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff on the meta-joke about Peng Lee. The viewer knows Artie thinks the bit stinks, so his cheerful 'It's terrific. I'm enjoying it.' is a pure lie that lands because of context. 'We should do this more often. I mean it.' from Larry, met with Artie's 'Absolutely,' is excruciating in the best way. High character integration — this dynamic is core to the show. The gap between performance and reality is the show's central comic engine. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: This whole disney thing has everybody shitting bricks, pins, and party favors.

jokes.text: Tell her to clean around me.
jokes.setup: Larry (calling Beverly at home) or Beverly's partner tells Beverly that Rosario is there to clean.
jokes.punchline: 'Tell her to clean around me.' — the sheer entitlement of this demand, delivered as if it's a reasonable request.
jokes.explanation: Five words of pure character comedy — the joke is entirely in the unreasonable entitlement delivered as if it's perfectly sensible. Very quotable, economical, and character-specific. The housekeeper subtext (Beverly has help) adds a class dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Of course not. I already told you I'm doing this for 5 years and then I'm getting out.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You're so deluded.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: OK. 8 years.

jokes.text: Oh. Warner's not gonna happen today. / Hey, sweetie, do you have to smoke the second you get up? / Yes, sweetie, I do. I'm an addict.
jokes.setup: Beverly's partner notes she's smoking immediately upon waking.
jokes.punchline: 'Yes, sweetie, I do. I'm an addict.' — Beverly's completely unapologetic, medically accurate self-description with zero shame.
jokes.explanation: The joke works through total ownership — Beverly doesn't defend herself or promise to quit, she simply states a clinical fact. The echo of 'sweetie' from partner to Beverly and back is a nice touch. Functional and charming but not remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: That's just the kind of Hollywood bullshit that makes me want to Chuck it all and join the peace corps. Yeah? Big bad Ron, you piece of shit! How's it going? Oh, fuck you, asshole.

jokes.text: Blow off Eiger and we'll spend the morning in bed. / Are you insane? I just got a 50% raise by pretending I was gonna go form my own agency. I can't stay in bed. People actually notice when I don't show up to work.
jokes.setup: Paula suggests blowing off an important Disney meeting to stay in bed.
jokes.punchline: 'People actually notice when I don't show up to work.' — Stevie's deadpan statement implies this is not the case for everyone in Hollywood, a quietly devastating insider joke about the industry's many passengers.
jokes.explanation: The 50% raise through a fake resignation bluff is a sharp industry detail, and the follow-up line implies a whole world of Hollywood sinecures. Good character writing, though it requires insider knowledge to fully appreciate.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Letterman can send 2 guys from bangladesh around the world and we can't send one Chinese guy to the movies?

jokes.text: This whole Disney thing has everybody shitting bricks, pins, and party favors.
jokes.setup: Stevie explains why he's stressed about the Disney corporate shakeup.
jokes.punchline: 'Shitting bricks, pins, and party favors' — an escalation of the 'shitting bricks' idiom that goes from painful to absurd with 'party favors,' suggesting the anxiety has a manic, almost festive quality.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely funny line — taking the 'shitting bricks' idiom and escalating it through three items that get progressively weirder. 'Party favors' is the key invention. It's a fresh extension of a cliché, delivered in character, and highly quotable. Near-8 territory for originality — the escalation pattern is clever wordplay that also characterizes Stevie's manic energy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's a... a parody of an asian-American judge, prancing around with twinkle-toed dinner theater rejects.

jokes.text: By the way, I can't go to Ojai this weekend because Eisner's taking the young turks to a Ducks game. / Are you gonna be like this the rest of your life? / Of course not. I already told you I'm doing this for 5 years and then I'm getting out. / You're so deluded. / OK. 8 years.
jokes.setup: Stevie cancels their weekend plans for an industry event. Paula asks if he'll always be like this.
jokes.punchline: 'Of course not. I already told you I'm doing this for 5 years and then I'm getting out.' / 'You're so deluded.' / 'OK. 8 years.' — the immediate revision of his own timeline under pressure is a perfect character moment.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is nearly perfect: firm assertion ('5 years and then I'm getting out'), immediate demolition ('You're so deluded'), and then Stevie's quiet capitulation ('OK. 8 years') — which doesn't even address the delusion, just negotiates the timeline. It's the 'snip snap' escalation in miniature — a man revealing his own lack of self-awareness through the act of adjusting his self-deception. Justifies 8+ for structure and character integration.

dialogue.line: Oh, and by, Dennis, by twinkle-toed, I imply nothing about their sexuality.

jokes.text: That's just the kind of Hollywood bullshit that makes me want to chuck it all and join the Peace Corps. / Yeah? Big bad Ron, you piece of shit! How's it going? / Oh, fuck you, asshole.
jokes.setup: Stevie complains about 'Hollywood bullshit' to Paula, positioning himself as above it all.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence his phone rings and he immediately drops the idealism to cheerfully greet someone with 'Big bad Ron, you piece of shit! How's it going?' — complete whiplash.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup (Stevie's Peace Corps fantasy) punctures the instant the phone rings — he goes from would-be idealist to hollering 'you piece of shit!' at a colleague without a breath in between. The structural contrast is executed perfectly. The aggressive greeting ('Big bad Ron, you piece of shit!') being used as a term of affection is itself a mini-joke about agent culture. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I had his sweet and sour chicken the other day, it was like hot pink. I think it's cough syrup. I swear to God.

jokes.text: We've received a substantial number of faxes and letters from the anti-defamation league protesting this segment that you're doing with Peng Lee. / Look, here's what I don't get. Letterman can send 2 guys from Bangladesh around the world and we can't send one Chinese guy to the movies?
jokes.setup: The network rep tells Larry they're getting anti-defamation complaints about Peng Lee.
jokes.punchline: Larry's defense: pointing to Letterman's 'Around the World' bit with two Bangladeshi men as evidence that NBC gets away with it, so CBS should too. The logic is both accurate and itself slightly offensive.
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-joke about real late-night show practices of the era — and Larry's competitive anxiety about Letterman bleeds into his defense of his own potentially offensive content. The 'Bangladesh' reference is historically accurate (Letterman really did have recurring bits with two Indian men). The irony that Larry defends Peng Lee by citing a comparable bit reveals his complete blindness to the actual issue. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: José jimenez was the first hispanic in space. Kids looked up to him. Well, he didn't actually go into space. That was just an act. Well, I believed it.

jokes.text: Indians do not watch television as much as Asians do, Larry. And besides, the Asian community is much more organized and vocal.
jokes.setup: Larry asks why Letterman gets away with his Indian-themed bits.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's cold calculus — the protest is not about ethics but about which community is better organized — is a nakedly cynical network executive's response.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the moral vacancy of the network executive — he's not saying the bit is wrong, just that Letterman's target audience complains less. This is a precise satire of institutional cowardice dressed as business strategy. The deadpan delivery of 'much more organized and vocal' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, then, you'll have a lot of screaming Japs picketing outside the studio. Screaming asian-americans.

jokes.text: Well, how does Leno get away with it? / He keeps putting on those damn Ito dancers. That's a parody of an Asian-American judge, prancing around with twinkle-toed dinner theater rejects.
jokes.setup: Larry keeps looking for precedents that prove he can run Peng Lee.
jokes.punchline: Artie's description of the Ito dancers (a real Leno recurring bit mocking Judge Lance Ito) as 'twinkle-toed dinner theater rejects' — which is a damning characterization of Leno's brand of comedy from Artie's old-school perspective.
jokes.explanation: 'Twinkle-toed dinner theater rejects' is a beautifully specific insult for the Ito dancers — accurate and vicious. The joke works on multiple levels: as Artie criticism, as Leno criticism, and as a comment on the whole late-night race-comedy landscape.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I sent Brian to the bank with my atm card, but I don't know what happened to him. He probably got sucked into some kind of parade.

jokes.text: Oh, and by, Dennis, by twinkle-toed, I imply nothing about their sexuality.
jokes.setup: Artie has just called the Ito dancers 'twinkle-toed.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate, unprompted clarification that he didn't mean to imply they were gay — which of course makes it sound like he absolutely did, while also parodying the 'no offense' hedge.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed beat — Artie's self-correction only draws attention to the implication. The joke is about the failure of the disclaimer, and Artie's total sincerity in offering it makes it funnier. Very Rip Torn — the character has enough authority that the correction sounds genuine while being ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It cured my cold.

jokes.text: Oh, come on, people. You know, in my day we had Amos and Andy. We had José Jimenez. José Jimenez was the first Hispanic in space. Kids looked up to him. / Well, he didn't actually go into space. That was just an act. / Well, I believed it.
jokes.setup: Artie defends ethnic comedy by invoking classic radio/TV characters from his era.
jokes.punchline: 'José Jimenez was the first Hispanic in space. Kids looked up to him.' / 'Well, he didn't actually go into space. That was just an act.' / 'Well, I believed it.' — Artie's sincere defense of a fictional space Hispanic reveals both his age and his total lack of critical distance.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest jokes. Artie's invocation of José Jimenez as a cultural role model, the revelation that Artie actually believed the fictional character was a real astronaut, and his total unselfconsciousness about it — 'Well, I believed it' — is perfect character comedy. It's absurd, specific, historically grounded (Bill Dana's José Jimenez was a real '60s character), and reveals Artie's worldview completely. 'Well, I believed it' is a devastating punchline delivered with complete sincerity. Justifies 8.5 easily.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What, is he only taking 10% of your love?

jokes.text: So it was not only funny, but it was inspirational as well.
jokes.setup: Artie has just established that he thought a fictional Hispanic character was a real astronaut.
jokes.punchline: Artie's summation: not only funny, but inspirational. The logic is completely circular — Artie inspired by a fictional achievement he mistook for real.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the José Jimenez joke — Artie's proud conclusion that the bit was both funny AND inspirational (since he was inspired by what he thought was a real Hispanic astronaut) is a lovely escalation of his obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: I want it to continue the way that it is except with more fucking.

jokes.text: Look, Larry, let's be clear here. We are not forcing you to do anything. We just strongly urge you to discontinue the piece. / And if I don't? / Well, then, you'll have a lot of screaming Japs picketing outside the studio. / Screaming Asian-Americans.
jokes.setup: The network strongly urges Larry to drop Peng Lee. Larry pushes back.
jokes.punchline: Dennis says 'screaming Japs' without blinking, then Artie immediately corrects to 'screaming Asian-Americans' — the correction from an ethnic slur to the politically correct term, delivered by the man who just invoked Amos and Andy.
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on the irony that the most politically incorrect man in the room (Artie, who just praised Amos and Andy) is the one who corrects the network suit's slur. The structural reversal — the show's defender of ethnic comedy enforcing PC language on the network guy — is both funny and a sharp institutional satire. The timing of Artie's correction is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Oh, my God, are you pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No, but it's nice to see what your reaction would be.

jokes.text: Hey, Phil... hey, great shirt! Where'd you get that? / Oh, thanks. I think I got it at... / Do you have a 20?
jokes.setup: Hank approaches Phil complimenting his shirt.
jokes.punchline: The shirt compliment was purely instrumental — Hank immediately asks for a $20 loan before Phil can finish answering the question about where he got the shirt.
jokes.explanation: A tight Hank joke — the fake compliment as social engineering is perfectly in character for his desperate-cheerful persona. The mid-sentence pivot (not even letting Phil finish his answer) is perfectly timed. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sure he'd be so thrilled to hear about Ed begley Jr.'s fucking electric car.

jokes.text: The last time I loaned you money, it took you like a month to pay it back. / I know, and you know what happened? I sent Brian to the bank with my ATM card, but I don't know what happened to him. He probably got sucked into some kind of parade.
jokes.setup: Phil is reluctant to loan Hank money because the last loan took a month to repay.
jokes.punchline: 'He probably got sucked into some kind of parade.' — Hank's explanation for why his assistant Brian disappeared with his ATM card is a totally absurd non-explanation delivered as if it's perfectly reasonable.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'He probably got sucked into some kind of parade' is a perfect piece of absurdist reasoning — it's not a specific parade, it's 'some kind of parade,' which makes it weirder and funnier. The word 'sucked' implies Brian had no agency in this parade situation. The confidence of Hank's delivery of an utterly incoherent explanation is quintessential Jeffrey Tambor character work. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: she, uh, got a really bad cold and she can't make it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I see, a cold.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's pretty serious.

jokes.text: No, I... I can't. I got the delivery guy from Peng's place. I ordered the sweet and sour chicken. / It's incredible. You ever had it? / It cured my cold.
jokes.setup: Hank explains he can't wait for Brian because the delivery man from Peng Lee's restaurant is there.
jokes.punchline: 'It cured my cold.' — Hank's endorsement of the sweet and sour chicken calls back to Dennis's suspicion that it tastes like cough syrup. The joke is that cough syrup = medicine = it cured his cold.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback. Dennis said the chicken tastes like cough syrup; Hank says it cured his cold. The logic is absurd but perfectly consistent, and it takes only three words to deliver the payoff. The economy is exceptional. The rewatch bonus is strong because it only fully lands if you remember Dennis's earlier line.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: She was skiing in Aspen and she, uh, got a really bad cold / and she can't make it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I see, a cold.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's pretty serious.

jokes.text: I don't even know why you go out with the guy, Paula. / I just do. I like him. / I know you don't 'cause you think he's rude on the phone. / Yes, he is. Because I have a name and he never uses it. / Who, Larry? / No, that Stevie.
jokes.setup: Beverly expresses skepticism about Paula's relationship.
jokes.punchline: Beverly assumes 'rude on the phone' refers to Larry (logical in context), but Paula means Stevie — a misdirection that also implies Larry is similarly rude on the phone.
jokes.explanation: A nice misdirection — Beverly's clarifying 'Who, Larry?' implies Larry is also someone who would plausibly be described as rude on the phone. The joke works because both characters are being critiqued simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The weather's so unpredictable this time of year when there's no snow.

jokes.text: Ah. What, is he only taking 10% of your love?
jokes.setup: Beverly is pressing Paula about Stevie's shortcomings as a boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: 'Is he only taking 10% of your love?' — Beverly applies the standard agent commission (10%) to the relationship, suggesting Stevie is emotionally underperforming at his own professional rate.
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp, economical joke. The 10% metaphor is industry-specific, genuinely witty, and perfectly succinct. Beverly applying agent economics to romantic performance is a clever character-world joke. The fact that it's Beverly — the show's most grounded character — making a sophisticated joke gives it extra texture. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Kindler
dialogue.line: Well, maybe you don't recognize me 'cause I'm a comic who never gets on TV. And why? Well, basically, thanks to people like you, that's why.

jokes.text: Oh, there's trouble in paradise. / So, is he running from commitment? / Are you making fun of me? / No, I'm not. Are you running from commitment? / You're making fun of me. / No. I just want to make sure that he's meeting your needs.
jokes.setup: Beverly pushes into Paula's relationship insecurities with mock-therapeutic language.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's patient repetition of 'Are you running from commitment?' while insisting she's not making fun — the joke is in Beverly's persistence and Paula's inability to accept sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the therapist-speak from Beverly is a bit on-the-nose and the exchange runs slightly long. The joke is about the dynamic rather than any particular line. Passable but not one of the episode's stronger moments.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My advice? Pepper spray, and don't be afraid to use it.

jokes.text: Hey, doll. Phil. / I'm gone.
jokes.setup: Stevie arrives to take Paula to lunch mid-conversation between Paula and Beverly.
jokes.punchline: Phil's immediate 'I'm gone.' — reading the room perfectly and exiting before things get complicated.
jokes.explanation: Two words perfectly delivered — Phil's instant self-extraction is a tiny, efficient joke about social intelligence. The economy is near-perfect but the joke itself is fairly light.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Jennifer sprained her ankle.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Really? You know, according to Paula, she mentioned to Artie that Jennifer has a head cold.

jokes.text: Come on. It's on the agency. Lunch with the booker of the Larry Sanders show. It's totally legit. Let's go liberate some money from the evil corporation.
jokes.setup: Stevie convinces Paula to go to lunch by framing it as a legitimate business expense.
jokes.punchline: 'Let's go liberate some money from the evil corporation.' — Stevie frames corporate expense account abuse as a heroic act of liberation, revealing his ability to moralize petty self-interest.
jokes.explanation: Stevie's self-romanticization as a rebel against corporate power while expensing a client lunch is a nice character note. Not a standout joke but good texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: OK, Hank, give him the money.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What money?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, there it is.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What are you... all you had to do was ask.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Prick.

jokes.text: How long have we been going out? / I don't know. 3 months. 4 months. / Well, gee, time flies when you're having fun. / What do you want out of this relationship? / Guess the fun's over.
jokes.setup: Stevie asks how long they've been dating, citing 3 or 4 months. Paula counters with 'time flies when you're having fun.'
jokes.punchline: 'Guess the fun's over.' — Stevie's response to the relationship-talk gambit is instant and dry.
jokes.explanation: A clean setup/punchline built out of a cliché. Paula uses 'time flies when you're having fun' and Stevie instantly weaponizes it: the relationship talk ending the fun. The timing and economy make it work.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: I walk around in my Italian suit all day like I'm on top of the world, but I'm a fake! And if I stop pretending for a second, I fall apart 'cause I'm terrified! I don't know what the fuck I'm doing.

jokes.text: I want it to continue the way that it is except with more fucking.
jokes.setup: Paula asks what Stevie wants out of the relationship. He pauses, then answers.
jokes.punchline: After the setup implies a possibly thoughtful answer, Stevie's response is 'more fucking' — the agent reduces the relationship to a negotiation with one dealbreaker item.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is very good — the beat/pause before the answer creates anticipation, and 'except with more fucking' is both the most honest thing Stevie could say and the most reductive. The fact that he frames it as 'except with' (incremental negotiation) rather than 'and' is perfect agent-brain syntax. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tell her about the suit.

jokes.text: What would you say if I told you I wanted to quit? / I don't know. Are you quitting? / Or if I said I wanted to have a baby? / Oh, my God, are you pregnant? / No, but it's nice to see what your reaction would be.
jokes.setup: Paula floats hypotheticals — quitting, having a baby — to gauge Stevie's reactions.
jokes.punchline: 'No, but it's nice to see what your reaction would be.' — Paula reveals the questions were tests. The punchline is Stevie's panicked 'are you pregnant?' being confirmed as exactly the reaction she wanted to document.
jokes.explanation: The trap-test dynamic is a familiar romantic comedy trope, but Paula's 'it's nice to see what your reaction would be' is a slightly chilling punchline — she's building a case. Works well because Stevie's panic is visible even in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: He is lame. Everybody in town thinks so. He's not funny.

jokes.text: Look, we have to go to lunch quick because your blood sugar is dropping.
jokes.setup: Paula is clearly in distress about their relationship. Stevie has just failed her hypothetical tests.
jokes.punchline: Stevie's response to emotional vulnerability is to diagnose it as a blood sugar problem and demand they go to lunch — the medicalizing of emotion as an escape mechanism.
jokes.explanation: A sharp character joke — Stevie avoiding emotional confrontation by reframing it as a physical medical symptom is a very specific and funny deflection. 'Your blood sugar is dropping' as a diagnosis for 'you're upset about our relationship' is both funny and a perfect character window.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Larry is the gorilla. He's huge, talent-wise.

jokes.text: How many of these clients would be up here if you and I weren't dating? / Jesus, Paula, I'm not going out with you to get my clients on the show. / That's good news. I guess you won't mind if I unbook Andy Kindler. / You can't do that. He's booked! / We've got a verbal contract. / I just did it.
jokes.setup: Paula questions whether Stevie books clients on her show because of their relationship.
jokes.punchline: The moment Stevie denies it, Paula immediately tests him by unbooked Andy Kindler — and Stevie's 'You can't do that. He's booked! We've got a verbal contract.' proves exactly that his concern IS professional, not personal. Paula's flat 'I just did it' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest dramatic-comic construction. Paula sets the trap, Stevie walks right into it, and the instant reversal from 'I'm not going out with you to get my clients on the show' to panicked defense of Kindler's verbal contract is a perfect revelation of character. 'I just did it' as a three-word punchline is devastating. The structure — denial, test, instant failure — is classically executed. Justifies 8.5.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Larry's the king, man. King Kong!

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ha ha ha ha! What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Where does an 800-pound gorilla sleep?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Anywhere he wants to.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't get it.

jokes.text: Bye, Jake Johannsen. These are good acts. / You know, I didn't force you to book them. I could've brought them to Letterman first. / Oh, I'm sure he'd be so thrilled to hear about Ed Begley Jr.'s fucking electric car.
jokes.setup: Stevie claims his clients are good and Letterman would want them too.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I'm sure he'd be so thrilled to hear about Ed Begley Jr.'s fucking electric car.' — Paula's specific, vicious imagining of what Ed Begley Jr. talks about on talk shows (his environmental obsession) is a perfect insider comedy insult.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Ed Begley Jr. (mentioned earlier as one of Stevie's clients) pays off brilliantly here. 'Ed Begley Jr.'s fucking electric car' as the ultimate unbook-able talk show pitch is a perfect insider joke — Ed Begley Jr. was famously evangelical about his electric car in the mid-90s. The specificity makes it sing. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jennifer Aniston
dialogue.line: Um, I'm... gosh, but I can't really think of anything I'd like to ask you at the moment. If I come up with something, I'll ask you later.

jokes.text: If you're gonna do that to them, then say good-bye to Jennifer Aniston. / You can't. / You can't unbook somebody who's booked for tonight. / I'll talk to you tonight. / No. I don't want to see you anymore. / Oh, I don't have time for this shit.
jokes.setup: The negotiation escalates — Stevie threatens to pull Jennifer Aniston; Paula ends the relationship.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I don't have time for this shit.' — Stevie's response to being broken up with is not hurt but logistical impatience. He literally doesn't have time for the relationship ending.
jokes.explanation: Stevie's inability to slow down even for a breakup is darkly funny character work. The joke is that ending the relationship is an inconvenience in a busy day — a sad and funny capsule of Hollywood relationship dynamics.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Hey, you... you didn't get back together with me just so you could get Jennifer aniston back on the show, did you?

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Of course not.

jokes.text: Um, she was skiing in Aspen and she, uh, got a really bad cold and she can't make it. / I see, a cold. / Yeah, it's pretty serious. / Yes, it is.
jokes.setup: Artie is told Jennifer Aniston canceled because she got a cold while skiing in Aspen.
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'I see, a cold' followed by the booker insisting 'it's pretty serious' and Artie's 'Yes, it is' — both characters performing sincerity about an obviously pretextual excuse.
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie deadpan — the slow, loaded repetition of the cover story ('a cold') as if testing its weight. Both participants knowing it's fake but maintaining the polite fiction is very show-biz and very Larry Sanders. The 'yes, it is' is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: You know how Larry's gonna feel when he hears about this? / Do we have to tell him?
jokes.setup: Artie describes the problem of Jennifer Aniston canceling.
jokes.punchline: 'Do we have to tell him?' — the immediate instinct to hide bad news from Larry, revealing the whole staff's relationship to his volatility.
jokes.explanation: A small but perfectly Larry Sanders beat — the staff's first instinct being to conceal information from the host rather than solve the problem. 'Do we have to tell him?' captures the whole show's backstage dynamic in six words.

jokes.text: Larry introduces the guest. They come out, they sit down. When that doesn't happen, Larry knows that something's wrong. Without a guest, Larry will sit here with his thumb up his ass.
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining to someone why they can't just not tell Larry about the missing guest.
jokes.punchline: 'Without a guest, Larry will sit here with his thumb up his ass.' — Artie's clinical description of the show's mechanics ends with a beautifully blunt image.
jokes.explanation: Artie's patient explanation building to a very Artie punchline — the formal setup followed by 'thumb up his ass' as the technical description of a host without a guest. Very Rip Torn — the vulgarity sounds clinical coming from him.

jokes.text: Skiing in Aspen. The weather's so unpredictable this time of year when there's no snow.
jokes.setup: Artie has been told Jennifer Aniston canceled because of a cold contracted while skiing in Aspen.
jokes.punchline: 'The weather's so unpredictable this time of year when there's no snow.' — Artie notes the impossibility of skiing in Aspen without snow, quietly demolishing the alibi.
jokes.explanation: One of Artie's best lines. The fake sincerity of 'the weather's so unpredictable' followed by the impossible qualifier 'when there's no snow' is a perfect deadpan demolition of a lie. It's gentle, devastating, and entirely in character — Artie never raises his voice, he just quietly notes the impossibility and lets it hang in the air. Justifies 8+ for structure, economy, and character integration.

jokes.text: I'm Andy Kindler. / Oh, my God, Andy. I'm sorry I didn't recognize you. / Well, maybe you don't recognize me 'cause I'm a comic who never gets on TV. And why? Well, basically, thanks to people like you, that's why.
jokes.setup: Andy Kindler shows up at the show after being booked and unbooked.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate pivot from introduction to accusation — 'thanks to people like you' delivered to Beverly, who has virtually no power in this situation — is a perfectly rendered portrait of a comedian at the end of his rope.
jokes.explanation: Andy Kindler playing an exaggerated version of himself is a nice meta-comedy touch (the real Andy Kindler was indeed this type of comedian). His specific grievance directed at Beverly — the wrong target — is funny because it's accurate to how powerless people absorb a comic's frustration.

jokes.text: Andy, do you know Beverly? / Mmm... excuse me. / I'm gonna go and eat up the rest of my cookie.
jokes.setup: Paula tries to introduce Beverly to Andy, who is mid-rant. Beverly sees what's coming.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's escape line — 'I'm gonna go and eat up the rest of my cookie' — is a perfectly timed exit delivered with total composure. The specificity of 'the rest of my cookie' makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna go and eat up the rest of my cookie' is a gem — the casual precision of 'the rest of' implies Beverly was in the middle of eating a cookie, had paused for this interaction, and is now returning to the task at hand. It's the exact right level of mundane specificity to be funny. Beverly is the show's secret weapon and this is one of her best exits. Justifies 8 for character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Listen, I don't make the final decisions around here, OK? / Oh, well, that's just bullshit. / Um, you know, maybe I could look at your tape again, if you want to leave it... with me.
jokes.setup: Paula tries to deflect Andy Kindler's accusations by saying she doesn't make final decisions.
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat 'that's just bullshit,' followed by Paula's deflation to 'maybe I could look at your tape again' — the industry's oldest brush-off, delivered with visible embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — 'maybe I could look at your tape again' as the industry's ultimate non-commitment is accurate and embarrassing. The pause implied before 'with me' adds to the deflation.

jokes.text: Hank, listen, I can't find Brian. / Well, join the club. / Do you have the money you owe me? / What money? / The $20 that I loaned you this morning. / Oh, right. See Brian about that.
jokes.setup: Phil tries to collect the $20 he loaned Hank earlier in the episode.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, right. See Brian about that.' — Hank has delegated the debt to his missing assistant, making it both literally impossible to collect and a perfect abdication of personal responsibility.
jokes.explanation: 'See Brian about that' — delegating a personal debt to a missing assistant — is a perfectly Hank move. The callback to Brian having vanished (probably into a parade) makes this land harder on rewatch. The escalating Brian subplot is a beautifully sustained running gag.

jokes.text: Hank, I can't find Brian, OK? That was my last $20, and I can't go to the cash machine after dark because I get mugged. / My advice? Pepper spray, and don't be afraid to use it.
jokes.setup: Phil explains why he needs the money back urgently — he gets mugged at ATMs at night.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response — 'Pepper spray, and don't be afraid to use it' — is simultaneously completely unhelpful (he still doesn't pay) and a piece of genuinely practical advice, delivered with the gravity of someone who has clearly used pepper spray.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the total absence of self-awareness — Hank's advice completely sidesteps the fact that he still hasn't repaid the money. 'Don't be afraid to use it' implies a hard-won wisdom that's funnier than any punchline he could offer. Very Jeffrey Tambor — the helpful-yet-useless mentor energy.

jokes.text: Jennifer sprained her ankle. / Really? You know, according to Paula, she mentioned to Artie that Jennifer has a head cold.
jokes.setup: Stevie offers a new excuse for Jennifer Aniston's cancellation — a sprained ankle.
jokes.punchline: The other person notes Paula already told Artie it was a head cold. The excuses are multiplying and contradicting each other — Jennifer Aniston apparently has both a cold and a sprained ankle and is skiing in Aspen.
jokes.explanation: The escalating web of contradictory excuses for Jennifer Aniston's absence is a running gag that rewards attention — the more excuses, the more obviously the whole thing fell apart because of the breakup. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: I walk around in my Italian suit all day like I'm on top of the world, but I'm a fake! And if I stop pretending for a second, I fall apart 'cause I'm terrified! I don't know what the fuck I'm doing.
jokes.setup: Stevie has apparently had a breakdown in Larry's office.
jokes.punchline: Stevie's raw confession — that his entire persona is performance — delivered with melodramatic sincerity, is both genuinely moving and deeply funny because it's 100% on-brand for a Hollywood agent.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the collision of authentic vulnerability with Hollywood artifice — Stevie's breakdown is real, but the confession ('I walk around in my Italian suit') is so industry-specific that it's also absurd. The 'Italian suit' as a symbol of fake confidence is a perfect detail.

jokes.text: Oh, are you upset about what happened? / Yeah. / Oh, now you're gonna get me upset. / Tell her about the suit. / Paula, I'm terrified. I built up these walls inside me, and I'm sorry, it's so hard for me to open up. / What about the suit?
jokes.setup: Paula and Stevie have an emotional moment in Larry's office. Larry observes.
jokes.punchline: 'Tell her about the suit.' / 'What about the suit?' — Larry, observing the emotional scene, keeps fixating on the Italian suit detail from Stevie's confession, reducing the breakdown to a fashion note.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest moment. Larry's interjection — 'Tell her about the suit' — in the middle of a genuine emotional reconciliation is a perfect capsule of his character: self-absorbed, slightly manipulative, and convinced he's helping. Paula's echo — 'What about the suit?' — completes it. Larry has turned someone else's emotional breakdown into a production note. The character integration is as complete as it gets on this show — only Larry Sanders would do exactly this. Justifies the high scores.

jokes.text: May I interrupt? / A Mr. Chen from the Asian-American Anti-Defamation League would like to talk to you about Peng Lee. / Is that the movie critic guy? / I wanted to say it, but I was afraid to, but he is lame. Everybody in town thinks so. He's not funny. / What do you think?
jokes.setup: Artie interrupts the emotional reconciliation scene to announce Peng Lee's critics are calling.
jokes.punchline: Paula's immediate 'I wanted to say it, but I was afraid to, but he is lame. Everybody in town thinks so. He's not funny.' — the news that anti-defamation groups are calling unlocks everyone's suppressed opinion of Peng Lee.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the running 'everyone knows he's not funny but won't say it' gag. The external pressure (anti-defamation league) triggers total candor in the room. The meta-irony — that it takes a formal complaint to get people to admit the bit is bad — is sharp.

jokes.text: Well, I think we oughta tell this, uh, pain in the ass from the anti-defamation league that we think that the remote is detrimental to the Asian community. / Yeah. It is. / It's smart. Good press. Right. Exactly.
jokes.setup: The group needs to respond to the anti-defamation league complaint.
jokes.punchline: Artie's solution — pretend they already thought the segment was harmful — turns a PR crisis into a PR opportunity. The instant group consensus ('Yeah. It is. / It's smart.') is a perfect corporate ethics parody.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the group's pivot from 'let's fight this' to 'let's take credit for canceling it' is a sharp institutional satire. 'It's smart. Good press.' captures how these decisions actually get made in television.

jokes.text: Peng Lee, Safeway. / Look how they fucked up their lives.
jokes.setup: Larry's summary response to the Peng Lee situation being resolved.
jokes.punchline: 'Peng Lee, Safeway. Look how they fucked up their lives.' — Larry apparently imagines Peng Lee going to work at Safeway after losing the TV gig, and his 'look how they fucked up their lives' implies his show was peng Lee's big break that Larry himself is now canceling.
jokes.explanation: Dark Larry comedy — he's both the cause of Peng Lee's professional ruin and the person lamenting it. The Safeway reference is a specific detail that makes the imagined fall vivid. 'Look how they fucked up their lives' as self-exculpating narration is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I got a last-minute phone call to do the show, then I get a phone call saying I'm not doing the show, then another phone call saying I am doing the show. / But, sweetie, you're here now and we couldn't be happier.
jokes.setup: Jennifer Aniston complains about the booking chaos to Larry backstage.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'But, sweetie, you're here now and we couldn't be happier.' — the most performative possible TV-host charm, used to deflect genuine grievance.
jokes.explanation: The talk-show charm being deployed as deflection is functional character comedy — Larry is performing host even offstage. Not a standout joke but consistent characterization.

jokes.text: Look at me. / Well, I certainly wouldn't be able to tell by the way I was treated today.
jokes.setup: Larry does his best host charm. Jennifer remains unimpressed.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's arch 'I certainly wouldn't be able to tell by the way I was treated today' — playing a slightly miffed version of herself and not letting Larry's charm fully work.
jokes.explanation: Jennifer Aniston playing herself as slightly diva-ish works because it's the right amount of edge. The line is functional; the meta-comedy of a real celebrity acknowledging the chaos of her own fictional booking is mild but pleasurable.

jokes.text: You got the Tiffany frame, didn't you? / Well, the only reason I'm doing this is because I'm dating Eddie. / Who's Eddie? / Eddie Ring, our sound man.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Jennifer got the gift (a Tiffany frame) — implying it was meant to smooth things over. Jennifer reveals she's only doing the show because she's dating a sound man.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer Aniston, the biggest star on the show, is appearing not for money or prestige but because she's dating the sound man — a perfect deflation of celebrity status.
jokes.explanation: A sharp joke about celebrity motivation — Jennifer Aniston is appearing on the Larry Sanders Show for love, not career reasons. The sound man as love interest is specifically funny because it's the most anonymous possible crew role. The Tiffany frame being mentioned alongside this revelation (gifts that don't actually work) adds texture.

jokes.text: Oh. You know, we also have a guy working on the show who's just a grip who's dating Sandra Bullock. / Donnie Padilla. He's in People magazine. He gets excited about that kind of stuff.
jokes.setup: Jennifer mentions dating the sound man. Larry one-ups her with his own crew-celebrity story.
jokes.punchline: 'He's in People magazine. He gets excited about that kind of stuff.' — Artie's mild, faintly condescending note about the grip's excitement about being in People magazine is a perfect class-consciousness joke.
jokes.explanation: 'He gets excited about that kind of stuff' — Artie's gentle condescension implies that people at his level don't get excited about People magazine. The joke works because Artie delivers it without malice, making it both funny and faintly sad.

jokes.text: What's this about a Tiffany frame?
jokes.setup: Larry asked Jennifer if she got the Tiffany frame. Now Hank, overhearing, wants to know about it.
jokes.punchline: Hank's plaintive 'What's this about a Tiffany frame?' — implying he didn't get one. The tiny moment of Hank feeling left out of the gift-giving is perfect insecure Hank.
jokes.explanation: This tiny moment is pure Hank — his identity is so wrapped up in being special that being excluded from a Tiffany frame feels personal. The question is asked with perfect bewildered hurt. Very Jeffrey Tambor, very specific to the character.

jokes.text: These are all, uh... are you all, uh, fans of Friends?
jokes.setup: Larry opens the interview with Jennifer Aniston by asking the studio audience if they're fans of Friends.
jokes.punchline: The question itself is slightly absurd — of course they're fans of Friends, she's on Friends — and the pause that presumably follows implies the audience's bemused reaction to such an obvious question.
jokes.explanation: A mild joke about Larry's tendency to state the obvious or fill space with awkward questions. The comedy is in his relentless need to perform rather than in any particular wit. Functional character beat.

jokes.text: Do you spend time with any one of them in particular off-camera? More than... yes, is one of them more than just a pen pal? / Well, wait, it's Friends. I meant friends.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Jennifer spends time with any cast member 'off-camera' — fishing for romantic gossip.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, wait, it's Friends. I meant friends.' — Larry confuses the show title 'Friends' with the concept of friendship, creating a momentary verbal tangle that he has to clarify.
jokes.explanation: The show-title-as-word confusion is a simple but effective bit — Larry gets tangled in the ambiguity of 'friends' vs. 'Friends,' which is a very plausible Larry moment. His recovery adds to the self-inflicted awkwardness.

jokes.text: Larry's the king, man. King Kong! Ha ha ha ha! What does that mean? / Where does an 800-pound gorilla sleep? / Anywhere he wants to. / I don't get it. / Larry is the gorilla. He's huge, talent-wise.
jokes.setup: Hank spontaneously shouts 'King Kong!' on the show during the Jennifer Aniston interview.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's genuine 'I don't get it' and the explanation 'Larry is the gorilla. He's huge, talent-wise.' — the gorilla joke explained kills it completely while also being a weirdly specific thing to have to explain.
jokes.explanation: The perfect callback payoff for Stevie's earlier 'King Kong!' — now Hank deploys it on the actual show, to a confused Jennifer Aniston. The joke paying off on live TV, requiring explanation ('Larry is the gorilla. He's huge, talent-wise.'), is the funniest possible outcome. Jennifer's genuine 'I don't get it' and the deadpan explanation make this one of the episode's strongest moments. Justifies 8.5 impact — the room would erupt.

jokes.text: What would you like to ask us? / Um, I'm... gosh, but I can't really think of anything I'd like to ask you at the moment. / If I come up with something, I'll ask you later. / Well, you're more than welcome to, uh, call in.
jokes.setup: Larry pivots the interview to Jennifer, inviting her to ask him questions.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer can't think of anything to ask Larry. Larry offers that she can 'call in' — as if they're running a radio show.
jokes.explanation: Jennifer's polite inability to think of anything to ask Larry — and Larry's earnest offer that she can 'call in' — is a gentle but effective riff on the asymmetry of the chat show interview. The 'call in' is a funny absurdist offer that implies the show will continue after she leaves.

jokes.text: Jennifer Aniston is doing so well. We got to get her back right away. / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Larry watches Jennifer's interview wrap and immediately pivots to rebooking her.
jokes.punchline: The instant calculation — the interview is barely over and Larry is already planning the next booking — is funny because it's simultaneously sincere and reveals his transactional relationship to all human interaction.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Larry's talent radar overrides all other instincts. Not a sharp joke on its own but serves the episode's final thematic note.

jokes.text: Hey, you... you didn't get back together with me just so you could get Jennifer Aniston back on the show, did you? / Of course not.
jokes.setup: Paula questions Larry's motives for helping smooth things over with Stevie — was it to get Jennifer Aniston back?
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Of course not.' — delivered with a beat of hesitation that implies the opposite. The perfect episode button: Larry may well have orchestrated the reconciliation for booking purposes.
jokes.explanation: The episode's perfect button. The question crystallizes the entire episode's theme — conflict of interest, where personal and professional are inseparable. Larry's 'Of course not' resolves nothing and everything. Given the title 'Conflict of Interest,' this is the thematic punchline on the whole episode. The ambiguity — is he lying? does he even know? — is the show's signature move. Structure and character integration are as good as they get. The best closing joke of the episode. Justifies 8.8.

tmdb_overview: Paula's dating Larry's agent, but Larry fears he's just using her to book his clients on the show. The network objects to Larry's ethnic guest spots. Hank tries to stiff Phil on a $20 loan.
